name: Combined work rate
derivation: A worker who finishes in $a$ days does $\frac1a$ of the work per day.
Working together, rates add: $\frac1a+\frac1b$ of the work per day.
Time for the whole job is 1 over the rate: $\frac1T=\frac1a+\frac1b$.
visual_proof: One tank split into units: the faster pipe fills more units each minute, and together they fill the sum of both shares every minute.
shortcut: Two workers: $T=\frac{ab}{a+b}$ (product over sum). If one is $k$ times faster than the other who takes $b$: $T=\frac{b}{k+1}$.

steps: Q's rate $=\frac1{110}$ per min; P is 21 times faster: $\frac{21}{110}$.

common_traps: Adding the times (or averaging them) instead of the rates.
Reading '21 times faster' as P's time = 21 × 110.
Forgetting to invert the combined rate to get time.

diagram.alt_text: A 110-unit tank: Q fills 1 unit and P fills 21 units per minute, 22 units per minute together, so 5 minutes of 22 units each.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)

def simulate(a, b):
    # standard: rates add; time = 1 / (1/a + 1/b)
    return 1 / (F(1, 1) / a + F(1, 1) / b)

n = 0
for _ in range(1500):
    a = F(random.randint(1, 500), random.randint(1, 4)); b = F(random.randint(1, 500), random.randint(1, 4))
    T = a * b / (a + b)
    assert T == simulate(a, b)
    assert T * (1 / a) + T * (1 / b) == 1
    assert T < min(a, b)
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-09_0900_Q07: Q 110 min, P 21 times faster -> 110/21 min
T = simulate(F(110, 21), F(110))
assert T == 5
assert {3, 4, 6} & {T} == set()
# 2024-09-09_0900_Q20: 17/27 in 34 days -> 54 days
assert F(34) / F(17, 27) == 54
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Total work as LCM; efficiency ratio
derivation: Take the total work as a number of units divisible by every time: $W=\mathrm{LCM}(t_i)$.
Efficiency is units per day: $e_i=\frac W{t_i}$, a whole number.
For fixed work, efficiency and time are inversely proportional: $e_1:e_2=t_2:t_1$.
Together time $=\frac W{\Sigma e_i}$, the same as $\frac1{\Sigma 1/t_i}$ but without fractions.
visual_proof: The job as a bar of W units; each worker's efficiency is how many units they shade per day.
shortcut: Given an efficiency ratio $e_1:e_2$ and joint time $T$: $W=(e_1+e_2)T$, then $t_1=\frac W{e_1}$.

steps: Faster is 2.5 times the slower: efficiencies $5:2$.

common_traps: Taking the faster pipe's time as $20\times2.5=50$ (multiplying time by the speed factor).
Writing efficiency ratio equal to time ratio instead of its inverse.
Using 2.5 : 1 for times rather than efficiencies (gives the slower pipe's time, 70 min).

diagram.alt_text: Tank of 140 units shared between pipes of efficiency 5 and 2 units per minute; together 7 per minute for 20 minutes.

verification.code:
import random
from math import lcm
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1500):
    k = random.randint(2, 4)
    t = [random.randint(1, 60) for _ in range(k)]
    W = lcm(*t)
    e = [W // ti for ti in t]
    assert all(W % ti == 0 for ti in t)       # whole-number efficiencies
    # time together with LCM units equals time from fractions
    assert F(W, sum(e)) == 1 / sum(F(1, ti) for ti in t)
    # efficiency ratio is inverse of time ratio
    assert F(e[0], e[1]) == F(t[1], t[0])
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-13_0900_Q07: rates 5 : 2 units, together 20 min
W = (5 + 2) * 20
fast = F(W, 5)
assert fast == 28
assert {34, 30, 32} & {fast} == set()
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Inlets and outlets: net rate
derivation: A filling pipe adds $\frac1{\text{fill}}$ of the tank per hour; a leak or outlet removes $\frac1{\text{empty}}$.
Open together, the net rate is inflow minus outflow.
Time to fill is 1 over the net rate: $\frac1T=\Sigma\frac1{\text{fill}_i}-\Sigma\frac1{\text{empty}_j}$.
If the net rate is 0 or negative, the tank never fills.
visual_proof: A tank of LCM units: the inlet adds units each hour, the leak takes some away, and the net units per hour set the filling time.
shortcut: Fill in $a$, with leak in $b$: leak alone empties in $\frac{ab}{b-a}$.

steps: Leak empties the full tank in 36 hours (A).

common_traps: Adding the leak's rate instead of subtracting it.
Answering 7.2 h by using $\frac{ab}{a+b}$ (the combined-fill formula).

diagram.alt_text: Tank of 36 units: the pipe adds 3 units per hour, the leak removes 1, net 2 per hour, filling in 18 hours; the leak alone empties 36 units in 36 hours.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)

def fill_time(fill, empty, step=None):
    net = sum(F(1) / f for f in fill) - sum(F(1) / e for e in empty)
    return None if net <= 0 else 1 / net

n = 0
for _ in range(1500):
    fill = [random.randint(1, 60) for _ in range(random.randint(1, 3))]
    empty = [random.randint(1, 120) for _ in range(random.randint(0, 2))]
    T = fill_time(fill, empty)
    if T is None:
        continue
    # after T, filled amount = sum of inflow - outflow = exactly one tank
    assert T * sum(F(1, f) for f in fill) - T * sum(F(1, e) for e in empty) == 1
    n += 1
# boundary: fill rate = empty rate -> tank never fills; just above -> very long but finite
assert fill_time([12], [12]) is None
assert fill_time([12], [13]) == 156
assert fill_time([12], [11]) is None
# worked example 2024-09-09_1600_Q23: fills in 12, with leak 18 -> leak alone 36
leak = 1 / (F(1, 12) - F(1, 18))
assert leak == 36
assert fill_time([12], [leak]) == 18
assert {F(72, 10), 63, F(36, 10)} & {leak} == set()
print(f"CASES={n}")
print("BOUNDARY_OK")

name: Joining, leaving and alternating
statement: \Sigma(\text{rate}_i\times\text{time worked}_i)=1;\ \text{alternating: work per cycle}=\Sigma\text{rates, then finish the remainder}
derivation: Each worker or pipe contributes rate $\times$ the time it actually worked.
The job is done when the contributions add to the whole: $\Sigma(\text{rate}_i\times t_i)=1$.
Alternating turns: one cycle (each takes one turn) does $\Sigma\text{rates}$.
Run whole cycles while work remains after them, then finish the remainder turn by turn in the same order.
visual_proof: A tank of 63 units filled in 2-hour cycles of 7 + 3 units: six cycles reach 60 units and X's next turn finishes the last 3.
shortcut: Joined/left problems: write each person's working time in terms of the unknown and solve one linear equation.

steps: One 2-hour cycle $=10$ units; 6 cycles (12 h) $=60$ units.
X finishes 3 units in $\frac37$ h: total $12\frac37$ h (D).

common_traps: Dividing 63 by 10 units per cycle as 6.3 cycles = 12.6 h: the last part is done by X alone at 7 units/h, not at the cycle average.
Using the combined rate as if both ran every hour (6.3 h).
Letting Y finish the remainder when it is X's turn.

diagram.alt_text: 63-unit tank: six 2-hour cycles of 10 units reach 60, then X fills the last 3 units in 3/7 hour.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)

def alternate(rates):
    # simulate hour by hour, taking turns in the given order
    done, t, i = F(0), F(0), 0
    while True:
        r = rates[i % len(rates)]
        if done + r >= 1:
            return t + (1 - done) / r
        done += r; t += 1; i += 1

def by_cycles(rates):
    # method: full cycles first, then finish the remainder turn by turn
    c = sum(rates)
    k = int((1 - F(1, 10**9)) // c)        # whole cycles that leave work remaining
    left, t = 1 - k * c, F(k * len(rates))
    for r in rates:
        if r >= left:
            return t + left / r
        left -= r; t += 1

n = 0
for _ in range(1200):
    rates = [F(1, random.randint(2, 40)) for _ in range(random.randint(2, 3))]
    assert alternate(rates) == by_cycles(rates)
    n += 1
# worked example 2024-09-19_0900_Q25: X 9 h, Y 21 h, alternate, X first
ans = alternate([F(1, 9), F(1, 21)])
assert ans == 12 + F(3, 7)
assert {10 + F(3, 7), 11 + F(3, 7), 9 + F(3, 7)} & {ans} == set()
# 2024-09-12_1230_Q14: A 48, B 66, tank full in 32 -> B closed after 22
assert (1 - F(32, 48)) * 66 == 22
print(f"CASES={n}")

name: Man-days-hours rule
derivation: With equal efficiency per man-hour, work done is proportional to total man-hours $M\times D\times H$.
So man-hours per unit of work is the same for both groups: $\frac{M_1D_1H_1}{W_1}=\frac{M_2D_2H_2}{W_2}$.
Cross-multiply and solve for the one unknown.
visual_proof: A table of men, days, hours and work for two groups; total man-hours per unit of work is the same in both rows.
common_traps: Putting W on the same side as M, D, H (inverts the answer).
Mixing groups with different efficiencies (women, boys) without converting them to men first.
Forgetting the hours-per-day factor when it changes between the groups.

diagram.alt_text: Table: 12 men, 10 days, 8 hours per day build 1 wall; 16 men working 6 hours per day need 10 days for the same wall.

verification.code:
import random
from fractions import Fraction as F
random.seed(0)
n = 0
for _ in range(1500):
    rate = F(random.randint(1, 50), random.randint(50, 500))   # work per man-hour, same for both groups
    M1, D1, H1 = random.randint(1, 60), random.randint(1, 60), random.randint(1, 12)
    W1 = M1 * D1 * H1 * rate
    M2, H2 = random.randint(1, 60), random.randint(1, 12)
    W2 = F(random.randint(1, 50), 7)
    D2 = W2 / (M2 * H2 * rate)                 # days needed from the work rate directly
    assert F(M1 * D1 * H1) / W1 == M2 * D2 * H2 / W2
    n += 1
# 12 men, 10 days, 8 h -> 1 wall; 16 men, 6 h/day -> 10 days for the same wall
assert F(12 * 10 * 8, 16 * 6) == 10
print(f"CASES={n}")
